Module 00 — Why Anatomy

What is Anatomy?

The study of structure — and how structure dictates function.

Not This
A List to Memorise
Hundreds of Latin names with no context. Forgotten by next week.
This
A Map to Navigate
A logical system where every name tells you something. Build it once — use it forever.

Anatomy isn't about memorisation. It's about building a mental model of the body you can think with.

Module 00 — Why Anatomy

Why It Matters For You

01
Better Exercise Selection
Know which muscles a movement actually trains — not just which muscles it's supposed to train.
02
Smarter Cueing
"Drive through the glute" lands differently when you know exactly where the glute attaches and what it does.
03
Clearer Communication
Talk to physios and doctors in their language. Your athlete gets better care when you're part of the conversation.
The bottom line: The coach who understands anatomy sees more, decides better, and communicates clearly — at every step.

First — let's learn how to learn anatomy. The method matters as much as the content.

Topic 01

How to
Learn
Anatomy

The method before the material. Learn this first — everything else gets easier.

Topic 01 — How to Learn Anatomy

The 3-Layer Method

Layer 1
Name It
What is it called? Where does the name come from?
Layer 2
Locate It
Where is it? What does it attach to? What surrounds it?
Layer 3
Apply It
How does it move? What exercises use it? What goes wrong?
Rule: Never move to Layer 2 until Layer 1 is solid. Never move to Layer 3 until Layer 2 is solid. Build, don't skip.
Topic 01 — How to Learn Anatomy

Tools That Actually Work

Sketch It
Drawing from memory cements it 10× faster than reading. You don't need to be an artist.
Move It
Feel the muscle working. Palpate origin and insertion on yourself while performing the movement.
Mnemonic It
"Tigers Love Licking Red Rabbits Sometimes" — one sentence, seven muscles. We use these throughout.
Rule of 3
Group muscles in threes. Wrist flexors, rotator cuff. Clusters beat isolated facts every time.

Context beats repetition. Always anchor a new muscle to a movement you already know.

Topic 01 — How to Learn Anatomy

What Not To Do

Avoid
Study in Isolation
Memorising names without knowing what they do or where they sit. The name is the last thing — not the first.
Avoid
Learn Everything at Once
650+ muscles exist. You need 40–50 for S&C competence. Prioritise: lower limb, spine, shoulder, upper limb.
Avoid
Skip the Framework
Jumping to muscle names without understanding planes and directions is like reading a map in a foreign language.
Topic 01 — Summary

Your Learning System

The Method
Name → Locate → Apply
Three layers, always in order. Never skip a floor.
The Tools
Sketch, Move, Mnemonic, Group
Active recall beats passive reading every time.
The Mindset
Context over memorisation
Every structure anchored to a movement you already coach.

Next — before we can name anything, we need to learn the language anatomy is written in.

Topic 02

The Language
of Anatomy

Terms, planes, directions, suffixes — the grammar of the body. Learn this once, decode anything.

Fig 1.7 — BD Chaurasia's Handbook of General Anatomy, 4th Ed.
Topic 02 — Language of Anatomy
Anatomical Position

The universal reference frame. Every anatomical description assumes this position.

Standing upright, eyes forward
Arms at sides, palms facing forward
Feet together, toes forward
When a physio says "anterior," they mean front relative to anatomical position — not how the athlete is currently positioned.
BD Chaurasia's Handbook of General Anatomy, 4th Ed.
Topic 02 — Language of Anatomy
Planes of Movement
SAGITTAL (Median)
Left/right divide. Flexion & Extension. Squat, deadlift, running stride.
FRONTAL (Coronal)
Front/back divide. Abduction & Adduction. Lateral raise, side lunge.
TRANSVERSE
Top/bottom divide. Rotation. Cable rotation, discus throw, golf swing.
Most athletic movements are multi-planar. A sprint combines all three simultaneously.
BD Chaurasia's Handbook of General Anatomy, 4th Ed.
Topic 02 — Language of Anatomy
Directional Terms I
SUPERIOR / INFERIOR
Above / Below. Head is superior to trunk.
ANTERIOR / POSTERIOR
Front / Back. Quads are anterior. Hamstrings are posterior.
MEDIAL / LATERAL
Toward / Away from midline. Adductors medial. IT band lateral.
IPSI / CONTRALATERAL
Same side / Opposite side. Key for diagonal movement patterns.
Coach tip: "Medial collateral ligament = inside of the knee." Inside = medial. Once you know medial, lateral follows.
BD Chaurasia's Handbook of General Anatomy, 4th Ed.
Topic 02 — Language of Anatomy
Directional Terms II
PROXIMAL / DISTAL
Closer / Farther from origin. Hip proximal to knee. Wrist distal to elbow.
SUPERFICIAL / DEEP
Toward / Away from surface. Skin is superficial. Bone is deep.
DORSAL / PALMAR
Back of hand / Palm side. Dorsum of foot = top of foot.
FLEXOR / EXTENSOR ASPECT
Side where flexion occurs. Biceps is on the flexor aspect of the arm.
Proximal/Distal trick: Think of a river — proximal is upstream (closer to source), distal is downstream.
Topic 02 — Language of Anatomy

Decoding Clinical Terms

-itisInflammation — Tendinitis, Bursitis, Fasciitis
-osisDegeneration — Tendinosis, Arthrosis
-algiaPain — Myalgia, Neuralgia
-trophyGrowth/wasting — Hypertrophy, Atrophy
-ectomySurgical removal — Meniscectomy
-plastySurgical repair — Arthroplasty
-rrhexisRupture — complete tear
-pathyDisease/disorder — Tendinopathy, Neuropathy

Next time a report says "patellar tendinopathy with femoral arthrosis" — you'll know exactly what that means.

Topic 02 — Language of Anatomy

The Muscle Decoder — Part 1

Every muscle name is a description. Learn the principles — decode any muscle.

Principle 01
Number of Origins
Biceps = 2. Triceps = 3. Quadriceps = 4.
Principle 02
Origin/Insertion Location
Sternocleidomastoid — Sternum + Clavicle → Mastoid.
Principle 03
Muscle Location
Tibialis anterior = front of tibia. Temporalis = temporal bone.
Try it: Flexor Carpi Radialis — Flexor (action) + Carpi (wrist) + Radialis (radial/thumb side). Decoded.
Topic 02 — Language of Anatomy

The Muscle Decoder — Part 2

Principle 04
Shape
Deltoid = triangle. Trapezius = trapezoid. Rhomboideus = rhombus.
Principle 05
Fiber Direction
Rectus = parallel. Oblique = at angle. Transverse = perpendicular.
Principle 06
Action
Flexor, Extensor, Abductor, Adductor — the action is in the name.
Principle 07
Size
Maximus (largest), Minimus (smallest), Longus / Brevis.

Quiz: "Extensor Carpi Ulnaris Brevis" = Extension + Wrist + Ulnar side + Short. Done.

Topic 02 — Summary

You Now Speak Anatomy

Reference Frame
Anatomical Position
The universal starting point. Every direction is relative to this.
The Grid
Planes + Directions
3 planes. 8 directional pairs. Every movement in this coordinate system.
The Code
Suffixes + Naming Principles
7 naming principles. Any term — any muscle — decoded.

Now that we speak the language — let's build the body. Starting from the ground up: the skeleton.

Topic 03

The Skeletal
System

206 bones. The scaffolding, the anchor points, and the lever arms — all in one system.

Topic 03 — The Skeletal System

Bone is Alive

Not passive scaffolding. Living tissue that adapts to the loads placed on it.

Wolff's Law
Bone grows and strengthens where it is stressed. Remove the stress — bone weakens. Apply progressive load — bone adapts. This is the biological basis of resistance training.
S&C Implication
High-impact and high-load training builds bone density. Gymnastics, weightlifting, and sprinting athletes have the highest bone mineral density of any sport group.
Bone Cells
Osteoblasts build bone. Osteoclasts break it down. Training tips the balance toward building — if load is appropriate and recovery is adequate.
Source: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 5th Ed., Ch.1
Source: eCampus Ontario — Open Educational Resources
Topic 03 — The Skeletal System
5 Types of Bone
LONG
Femur, humerus — levers for movement. Longest bones in the body.
SHORT
Carpals, tarsals — stability over range of motion.
FLAT
Sternum, scapula — protection + large muscle attachment surface.
IRREGULAR
Vertebrae — complex shape serves a complex function.
SESAMOID
Patella — embedded in tendon, changes force angle of the quad.
The patella increases the quad's mechanical advantage by redirecting the angle of pull on the tibia.
BD Chaurasia's Handbook of General Anatomy, 4th Ed.
Topic 03 — The Skeletal System
Bone Landmarks — Upper Limb

Named features on bones where muscles attach, nerves pass, or joints form. Your anatomical navigation points.

TUBERCLE / TUBEROSITY
Rounded bump — muscle attachment. Greater tubercle of humerus = rotator cuff insertion.
EPICONDYLE
Above the condyle. Medial epicondyle = golfer's elbow. Lateral = tennis elbow.
CONDYLE
Rounded articular surface — forms part of a joint.
FOSSA
Depression or hollow. Infraspinous fossa = infraspinatus origin.
When a physio says "lateral epicondylalgia" — that's the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. You now know exactly where that is.
Topic 03 — The Skeletal System

Bone Landmarks — Lower Limb

Source: bettybroadbent.com
Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica
GREATER / LESSER TROCHANTER
Femur. Greater = glute max insertion. Lesser = iliopsoas insertion.
LINEA ASPERA
Posterior ridge of femur. Origin for adductors + short head of biceps femoris.
TIBIAL TUBEROSITY
Patellar tendon attachment. Osgood-Schlatter affects this in adolescent athletes.
MALLEOLI
Medial (tibia) + lateral (fibula) malleolus — key ankle sprain reference points.
Source: Labster Theory — theory.labster.com
Topic 03 — The Skeletal System
Axial vs Appendicular
AXIAL — 80 bones
Skull, vertebral column (C1–coccyx), ribs, sternum. The central core. Protects the CNS and vital organs.
APPENDICULAR — 126 bones
Shoulder girdle, arms, hands, pelvis, legs, feet. Where S&C happens. The levers that generate and express force.
S&C coaches focus primarily on the appendicular skeleton + spine. Head and visceral anatomy deprioritised in our practice.
Topic 03 — Summary

The Skeleton — Your Takeaway

Living Tissue
Bone Adapts
Wolff's Law. Load it progressively — it gets stronger. Remove load — it weakens. Training is the stimulus.
5 Types
Shape = Function
Long = levers. Short = stability. Flat = protection. Sesamoid = mechanical advantage.
Landmarks
Navigation Points
Tubercles, condyles, epicondyles, fossae — every muscle attaches somewhere. These are the addresses.

Bones don't move on their own. They need joints — the next topic.

Topic 04

Joints

Where two bones meet — and where movement is made possible or restricted.

Topic 04 — Joints

What is a Joint?

Any point where two bones meet. Structure determines how much movement is possible.

Type 1
Fibrous
Bones joined by fibrous tissue. No movement. Sutures of the skull. Not relevant to athletic movement.
Type 2
Cartilaginous
Bones joined by cartilage. Limited movement. Intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis. Shock absorption role.
Type 3
Synovial
Most joints in the body. Free movement. Hip, knee, shoulder, elbow. This is where S&C happens.
Source: NSCA 5th Ed., Ch.1 — "Movements in sport and exercise mainly occur at synovial joints."
BD Chaurasia's Handbook of General Anatomy, 4th Ed.
Topic 04 — Joints
Inside a Synovial Joint
ARTICULAR CARTILAGE
Hyaline cartilage covers bone ends. Smooth, low-friction. Avascular — doesn't heal well. Protect it.
JOINT CAPSULE
Fibrous sleeve surrounding the joint. Reinforced by ligaments. Provides stability.
SYNOVIAL MEMBRANE
Lines the capsule. Produces synovial fluid — the joint's lubricant and nutrient delivery system.
SYNOVIAL FLUID
Nourishes cartilage. Movement pumps this fluid — "motion is lotion."
Key insight: Cartilage has no blood supply. It gets nutrition from synovial fluid — which requires movement. Immobility starves cartilage.
Source: eCampus Ontario — Open Educational Resources
Topic 04 — Joints
6 Synovial Joint Types
PIVOT
Rotation only. C1/C2 — head rotation. Radioulnar — pronation/supination.
HINGE
Flexion/extension only. Elbow, ankle. One plane of movement.
CONDYLOID
Two planes. Wrist — flexion/extension + side-to-side deviation.
SADDLE
Two planes + rotation. Thumb CMC — unique to humans.
PLANE/GLIDING
Small gliding movements. Tarsal bones, AC joint, facet joints.
BALL & SOCKET
All 3 planes. Hip and shoulder — maximum range, maximum injury risk.
More range = less stability. The shoulder can do almost anything — and dislocates more than any other joint. Range and stability always trade off.
Topic 04 — Joints

Stability vs Mobility

Every joint sits on a spectrum. Understanding where a joint sits tells you how to train it.

Needs Mobility
Ankle
Restricted dorsiflexion = compensations at knee, hip and spine.
Needs Stability
Knee
Hinge joint. Excessive rotation = injury. Valgus collapse = ACL risk.
Needs Mobility
Hip
Ball-and-socket. Restricted hip forces lumbar spine to compensate.
Needs Stability
Lumbar
5 vertebrae. Load transfer and stability — not rotation. Rotation under load = disc risk.
Needs Mobility
Thoracic
12 vertebrae. Designed for rotation. Trunk rotation in throwing comes from here.
Needs Mobility
Shoulder
Most mobile joint. Needs rotator cuff for dynamic stability.

Joint-by-joint principle: alternating mobile and stable joints up the chain. Restrict one — the next joint takes the stress.

Topic 04 — Summary

Joints — Your Takeaway

3 Types
Fibrous, Cartilaginous, Synovial
Synovial joints = where sport happens. Capsule, cartilage, fluid — all essential.
6 Shapes
Shape = Permitted Movement
Hinge = one plane. Ball-and-socket = three planes. Structure always dictates function.
The Trade-off
Range vs Stability
More mobile joints need more muscular support. Train the tissue that protects the joint.

Joints are held together and moved by soft tissues — cartilage, tendons, ligaments, and fascia. That's next.

Topic 05

Soft
Tissues

Cartilage, tendons, ligaments, fascia — the connective tissue framework that holds everything together.

Source: ResearchGate — Histological differences between cartilage types
Topic 05 — Soft Tissues
3 Types of Cartilage
HYALINE CARTILAGE
Covers articular surfaces. Smooth, low-friction. Avascular — doesn't heal well. Once damaged, rarely fully recovers. Prevention over treatment.
FIBROCARTILAGE
Meniscus, intervertebral discs. Resists compression and shear. Some healing capacity. Most common in S&C injury contexts.
ELASTIC CARTILAGE
Ear, epiglottis. Flexible, maintains shape. Least relevant to S&C practice.
Critical: Hyaline cartilage has no blood supply — gets nutrition from synovial fluid only. Protect it through load management and adequate movement.
Source: Knya Medical — knyamed.com
Topic 05 — Soft Tissues
Tendon vs Ligament
TENDON — Muscle to Bone
Transmits contractile force. Dense, parallel collagen fibres. Injury = strain or tendinopathy. Achilles, patellar tendon, rotator cuff tendons.
LIGAMENT — Bone to Bone
Stabilises joints passively. Less organised collagen. Injury = sprain. ACL, MCL, lateral ankle ligaments.
STRAIN — muscle or tendon. Grade 1/2/3.
SPRAIN — ligament. Grade 1/2/3.
Topic 05 — Soft Tissues

Injury Grading

Strain — Muscle / Tendon
Source: Pure Dynamic Osteopathy
Sprain — Ligament
Source: Princess Alexandra Hospital NHS Trust
GRADE 1
Minor tears. Full function. Pain on palpation only. Return: days–1 week.
GRADE 2
Partial tear. Moderate loss of function. Pain + swelling. Return: weeks.
GRADE 3
Complete rupture. Full loss of function. May need surgery. Return: months.
Anatomy Trains — Thomas W. Myers, 3rd Ed.
Topic 05 — Soft Tissues
Fascia — The Forgotten Tissue

Standard anatomy presents muscles as individual units — bone to bone, origin to insertion. This is an artifact of how we dissect. Not how the body actually works.

THE REALITY

Muscles are embedded in a continuous fascial web. Force is transmitted through fascia between muscles — not just from muscle to bone. A tight calf can create tension that travels all the way into the lumbar spine.

"Whatever else they may be doing individually, muscles also influence functionally integrated body-wide continuities within the fascial webbing."
— Thomas W. Myers, Anatomy Trains, 3rd Ed.
Topic 05 — Soft Tissues

Myofascial Lines

The body works in connected chains — not isolated muscles. Two lines every S&C coach needs to know.

Anatomy Trains — Thomas W. Myers, 3rd Ed.
Anatomy Trains — Thomas W. Myers, 3rd Ed.
SUPERFICIAL BACK LINE
Plantar fascia → Achilles → Hamstrings → Sacrotuberous ligament → Erectors → Suboccipitals.
Tight calf = tight hamstring = low back tension.
SUPERFICIAL FRONT LINE
Tibialis anterior → Quads → Rectus abdominis → Sternocleidomastoid.
Anterior chain tension = forward head posture.
S&C application: Chronic hamstring tightness? Check the calf and plantar fascia first. The problem may not be where the symptom is.
Topic 05 — Summary

Soft Tissues — Your Takeaway

Cartilage
Hyaline Doesn't Heal
No blood supply. Prevention is the only reliable treatment. Protect articular surfaces through load management.
Tendons & Ligaments
Strain vs Sprain
Tendon = muscle to bone (strain). Ligament = bone to bone (sprain). Grade 1/2/3 — same scale, different tissue.
Fascia
The Body Works in Lines
Force transmits through fascial chains. A problem in one region creates tension elsewhere. Think in chains, not muscles.

The engine that drives everything: muscles. That's next.

Topic 06

Muscles

Structure, architecture, fiber types, actions, and the mnemonics that make them stick.

Source: StoryMD — storymd.com
Topic 06 — Muscles
The Russian Doll

Every muscle is a nested hierarchy of connective tissue. Smallest to largest:

Endomysium — wraps each individual muscle fiber
Perimysium — wraps bundles of fibers (fascicles)
Epimysium — wraps the entire muscle (deep fascia)
Tendon — epimysium continues as tendon → bone periosteum
All three layers are continuous with the tendon. Tension in any fiber is transmitted through the entire hierarchy to bone. Source: NSCA 5th Ed., Ch.1
Source: ScienceDirect — sciencedirect.com
Topic 06 — Muscles
Muscle Architecture

How fibers are arranged determines what a muscle is optimised for — force or speed and range.

PARALLEL (incl. Fusiform)
Fibers run along the axis of pull. Greater ROM and faster shortening. Sartorius, biceps brachii. Speed and range.
PENNATE (Uni / Bi / Multi)
Fibers at an angle to the axis. More fibers packed in = greater force. Rectus femoris (bi), deltoid (multi), tibialis posterior (uni).
CONVERGENT / CIRCULAR
Pectoralis (fan-shaped). Orbicularis (sphincter — closes the eye or mouth).
Rule: Pennate = power. Parallel = speed and range. Quads (bipennate) generate enormous force but fatigue quickly.
NSCA Essentials of Strength Training & Conditioning, 5th Ed. — Fig 1.9
Topic 06 — Muscles
Muscle Fiber Types
TYPE I — Slow Twitch
High fatigue resistance. Aerobic. Low force output. Marathon, cycling, postural muscles.
TYPE IIa — Fast Twitch (Intermediate)
Moderate fatigue resistance. Aerobic + anaerobic. 800m, team sports, repeated sprints.
TYPE IIx — Fast Twitch (Power)
Fatigues quickly. Anaerobic. High force + power. 100m sprint, Olympic lifting, throwing.
Size Principle: Motor units recruited smallest first (Type I), then progressively larger (IIa → IIx). Heavy loads recruit all types. Light loads recruit only Type I.
Topic 06 — Muscles

Actions & Roles

Types of Contraction
CONCENTRIC
Muscle shortens under tension. Curling up. The "lifting" phase.
ECCENTRIC
Muscle lengthens under tension. Lowering the weight. Greatest injury prevention value.
ISOMETRIC
No length change. Holding a plank, grip, stabilisation.
Roles in Movement
AGONIST
Primary mover. Quads in a squat.
ANTAGONIST
Opposes the agonist. Hamstrings during a squat — regulates and decelerates.
SYNERGIST
Assists the agonist. Glutes + calves assist quads in a squat.
STABILISER
Fixes a joint so others can move. Core in any loaded movement.

Eccentric training is the most underused tool in injury prevention. Prioritise it.

Topic 06 — Muscles

Origin, Insertion & Innervation

Origin
Fixed End
Usually proximal. Doesn't move during a standard contraction.
Biceps Femoris: Ischial tuberosity (long head).
Insertion
Moving End
Usually distal. The part that moves when the muscle contracts.
Biceps Femoris: Head of fibula.
Innervation
The Control Wire
Which nerve controls this muscle.
Biceps Femoris: Sciatic nerve — tibial division (long head), peroneal (short head).
Why innervation matters: If the sciatic nerve is irritated, the hamstrings may test weak — but the muscle is fine. The nerve is the issue. Know the nerve → identify the real problem.
The exception: In open chain movement, origin and insertion can reverse. Leg press — tibia is fixed, femur moves. Insertion becomes the functional origin.

Topic 06 — Summary

Muscles — Your Takeaway

Structure
Russian Doll Hierarchy
Endomysium → Perimysium → Epimysium → Tendon → Bone. All continuous. All load-bearing.
Architecture
Pennate = Force, Parallel = Speed
Fiber angle determines what the muscle is built for. Architecture is destiny.
Control
The Nerve Drives Everything
Origin, insertion, innervation. A muscle is only as good as its nerve supply. Next: the control system.

The muscle is the engine. The nerve is the ignition. Next — nerves and innervation.

Topic 07

Nerves &
Innervation

The control system — motor units, nerve maps, dermatomes, and what referred pain tells you.

Source: eCampus Ontario — Open Educational Resources
Topic 07 — Nerves & Innervation
The Motor Unit
DEFINITION
One motor neuron + all the muscle fibers it controls. When the neuron fires — all fibers in that unit contract simultaneously. All-or-none principle.
RECRUITMENT
Light loads recruit small motor units (Type I). Heavy loads recruit progressively larger (IIa → IIx). Heavy training creates full-spectrum adaptation.
RATE CODING
More force = higher firing frequency. Early training gains are largely neural — better recruitment before hypertrophy occurs.
Source: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training & Conditioning, 5th Ed., Ch.1
Topic 07 — Nerves & Innervation

Nerve Maps — Upper & Lower Limb

Source: TeachMeAnatomy — teachmeanatomy.info
Source: baby-blocks.com
Key S&C Nerves
Radial
Wrist/finger extensors. Compression = wrist drop.
Ulnar
Intrinsic hand muscles. "Funny bone" at elbow.
Median
Forearm flexors + thumb. Carpal tunnel.
Femoral
Quadriceps. Weakness = quad inhibition.
Sciatic
Hamstrings + all below knee. Most commonly irritated nerve in S&C.
Common Peroneal
Tibialis anterior. Compression = foot drop.
Source: Wikipedia — Dermatome (anatomy)
Topic 07 — Nerves & Innervation
Dermatomes & Referred Pain

A dermatome is a patch of skin whose sensation is controlled by a single spinal nerve. Pain in a dermatome tells you which spinal level is involved.

L4 / L5 / S1 — CLASSIC SCIATICA
Pain, numbness or tingling down the back of the leg into the calf and foot. Not a hamstring problem — a nerve problem.
C6 / C7 — CERVICAL RADICULOPATHY
Numbness into thumb (C6) or middle finger (C7). Pain in the arm — but the source is the neck.
THE COACH RULE
If pain travels along a predictable path and is influenced by neck or back position — it's likely neural, not muscular. Refer appropriately.
Topic 07 — Summary

Nerves — Your Takeaway

Motor Unit
One Nerve, Many Fibers
All-or-none. Recruitment follows the size principle. Heavy training recruits the full spectrum.
Nerve Maps
Know Your Key Nerves
Sciatic, femoral, radial, ulnar, median. Weakness or pain in a territory = suspect the nerve first.
Dermatomes
Pain Travels Predictably
Symptoms in a dermatome pattern = spinal level involvement. Don't treat the symptom — find the source.

One more topic — and possibly the most practically useful one: what pain actually is.

Topic 08

Pain
Science

What pain actually is — and why this changes how you talk to injured athletes.

Source: Rehab Science — Tom Walters (2023)
Topic 08 — Pain Science
Pain Comes From The Brain
OLD MODEL (Descartes, 1644)
Tissue damage → pain signal → brain. Simple cause and effect. Touch fire = pain.
MODERN UNDERSTANDING
The brain receives danger signals and decides whether to produce pain. Pain is a protection output — not a direct readout of tissue damage.
→
30–80% of people with bulging discs on MRI feel no pain.
→
People feel pain in amputated limbs — no tissue, real pain.
→
Tissue damage ≠ pain level. Pain ≠ tissue damage. Context matters enormously.
Source: Rehab Science — Tom Walters (2023), Ch.1
Topic 08 — Pain Science

What This Means For Coaches

Principle 01
Don't Catastrophise
An MRI finding is not a sentence. "You have a bulging disc" does not mean "you can't train." Language shapes the pain experience — choose your words carefully.
Principle 02
Movement is Medicine
Prolonged rest increases fear of movement and deconditions tissue. Graded exposure within pain tolerance accelerates recovery for most musculoskeletal conditions.
Principle 03
Know Your Limits
Pain science is not a reason to dismiss pain. Severe, sudden, or neurological pain requires medical referral. Your role is to keep athletes moving — not to diagnose.

Pain is information — not a verdict. Help your athletes understand this, and recovery changes.
